questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, what is the defining characteristic of artificial intelligence (AI) as a category?

options.A: It requires the use of deep neural networks with many layers
options.B: It performs tasks that would otherwise be considered to require human intelligence
options.C: It learns exclusively from labeled training data rather than hand-written rules
options.D: It produces original content rather than merely classifying existing content

questions.explanation: AI is defined in capability-based terms: any system that performs a task otherwise thought to require human intelligence, regardless of the underlying technique. Option A describes deep learning specifically, a much narrower subset of AI. Option C describes machine learning, which learns from data rather than AI as a whole. Option D describes generative AI, a further subset within deep learning. AI itself does not require any particular mechanism.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: Which of the following best distinguishes machine learning from AI in general, as described in the chapter?

options.A: Machine learning systems improve performance by learning patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules
options.B: Machine learning systems must be based on neural networks with multiple layers
options.C: Machine learning refers only to systems that generate new content rather than classify it
options.D: Machine learning is a marketing term with no meaningful technical distinction from AI

questions.explanation: Machine learning is the subfield of AI in which a system improves performance by learning patterns from data, illustrated by a spam filter trained on labeled emails rather than hand-written rules. Option B describes deep learning, a narrower subset of ML. Option C describes generative AI, not machine learning generally. Option D is incorrect; the chapter treats the ML/AI distinction as economically significant because it changes what you actually pay for.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the relationship among artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and neural networks?

options.A: They are four separate, unrelated approaches to building intelligent systems
options.B: Neural networks are a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of AI but not of machine learning
options.C: Machine learning is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of AI
options.D: Each narrower term nests inside the broader one: deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI, and neural networks are the mechanism deep learning is built on

questions.explanation: The chapter describes these terms as nesting like Russian dolls: every neural network is deep learning, every deep learning system is machine learning, and every machine learning system is AI, but never the reverse. Option A ignores this nesting entirely. Option B skips over machine learning in the chain. Option C reverses which term contains which.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: What distinguishes a generative AI model from a discriminative model?

options.A: A generative model sorts inputs into predefined categories, while a discriminative model produces new examples
options.B: A generative model requires no training data, while a discriminative model requires labeled data
options.C: A generative model learns the underlying pattern of a class of data well enough to produce new, original examples, while a discriminative model sorts inputs into categories
options.D: There is no meaningful difference; the terms are interchangeable

questions.explanation: A generative AI model learns a class of data's underlying pattern well enough to produce new, original examples, while a discriminative model sorts inputs into existing categories, such as flagging spam or fraud. Option A reverses these two definitions. Option B is false; both approaches require training data. Option D is incorrect because the chapter treats this distinction as economically important, since generation requires substantially more computation than classification.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: Why does processing a longer passage of text cost substantially more than twice as much when its length is doubled, according to the chapter's discussion of self-attention?

options.A: Longer passages require more pretraining data to be collected in advance
options.B: Self-attention compares every word in the passage against every other word, so computation grows faster than the text length itself
options.C: Longer passages always require a larger model with more parameters
options.D: The model must fine-tune itself on the fly for each new passage it processes

questions.explanation: Because self-attention compares every word against every other word, the computation it requires grows faster than the length of the input text, so doubling a passage's length more than doubles the processing cost. Option A confuses this with data collection for pretraining, an unrelated stage. Option C incorrectly ties passage length to parameter count. Option D describes fine-tuning, which does not occur automatically during inference.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: What happens during the pretraining stage of a large language model's development?

options.A: The model is adjusted using human preference comparisons between pairs of responses
options.B: The model is trained on a small, domain-specific dataset such as a company's support transcripts
options.C: The model is taught to treat prompts as instructions rather than text to continue
options.D: The model is exposed to a massive, general corpus of text and learns broad language patterns by repeatedly predicting the next word

questions.explanation: Pretraining is the first and most expensive stage, in which a model is exposed to a massive, general corpus of text and learns grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns by repeatedly predicting the next word. Option A describes RLHF alignment. Option B describes fine-tuning on a smaller, domain-specific dataset. Option C describes instruction tuning. Each of these later stages builds on, and costs far less than, pretraining.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: How does RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) alignment differ from instruction tuning?

options.A: RLHF refines model behavior using human preference judgments between response pairs, while instruction tuning trains on fixed instruction-response examples
options.B: RLHF is a stage that occurs before pretraining, while instruction tuning occurs after
options.C: RLHF trains an entirely new, smaller model, while instruction tuning compresses an existing model's parameters
options.D: RLHF and instruction tuning are two names for the exact same process

questions.explanation: RLHF alignment refines a model's behavior using human judgments about which of two responses is preferred, while instruction tuning trains on fixed pairs of instructions and correct responses. Option B misstates the sequence; both stages occur after pretraining. Option C describes an unrelated model-compression technique, not either of these fine-tuning stages. Option D wrongly treats the two stages as identical, when they use different training signals.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: A foundation model costs $10 million to pretrain and a fraction of a cent per query to run. What is the underlying reason its cumulative inference cost can eventually exceed its one-time training cost?

options.A: Inference requires more GPU memory per request than training does
options.B: Providers deliberately price inference higher than training to recover costs faster
options.C: Inference is a small, recurring per-request expense that accumulates without limit as usage volume grows, while training is a one-time cost
options.D: Training costs are refunded once a model reaches a certain number of users

questions.explanation: Training is typically a one-time or infrequent expense, while inference is a small per-request cost that recurs on every single use; at sufficient usage volume, the accumulated inference cost surpasses the one-time training cost. Option A misattributes the cause to memory requirements rather than cost structure. Option B assumes a deliberate pricing strategy the chapter does not describe. Option D describes a refund mechanism that does not exist.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: What does a model's context window determine?

options.A: The total number of parameters the model has learned during training
options.B: Whether the model can process images in addition to text
options.C: The organization that hosts and provides access to the model
options.D: The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider at once, including both the prompt and its response

questions.explanation: The context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can consider at once, covering both the prompt sent to it and the response it generates. Option A describes model parameter count, a distinct measure of learned scale. Option B describes multimodal capability. Option C describes the role of a model provider. None of these concern how much text a model can process in a single request.

questions.chapter: Core Concepts of Large Language Models
questions.question_text: A small startup wants to deploy a large language model quickly but has no engineering staff available to provision or maintain GPU infrastructure. Based on the trade-offs described in the chapter, which deployment approach best fits this situation?

options.A: Download an open-source model's weights and host it on self-managed infrastructure
options.B: Access a proprietary model through a provider's API endpoint, accepting a higher per-call price in exchange for no hosting burden
options.C: Pretrain a new foundation model from scratch to have full control over costs
options.D: Use a purely rule-based system instead of a large language model

questions.explanation: A proprietary model accessed through a provider's API endpoint trades a higher per-call price for zero hosting burden, which fits a team without infrastructure capacity. Option A requires exactly the in-house engineering effort the startup lacks. Option C describes pretraining a foundation model from scratch, an enormously expensive undertaking unrelated to quick deployment. Option D abandons generative AI capability entirely, which does not meet the stated need.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: What is a system prompt?

options.A: The end user's specific question submitted in a single request
options.B: A numerical representation of a piece of text used for similarity search
options.C: A persistent segment of instructions, usually invisible to the end user, that sets the model's role, tone, and constraints for the whole conversation
options.D: The retrieved text a RAG system inserts into a prompt

questions.explanation: The system prompt is a persistent, usually invisible segment that sets the model's role, tone, and constraints across an entire conversation, and it is typically resent with every request. Option A describes an ordinary user prompt, not the persistent instruction layer. Option B describes an embedding. Option D describes retrieved context in a RAG pipeline, a separate mechanism entirely.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: What is prompt engineering?

options.A: The practice of deliberately designing prompts to reliably get better, more accurate, or more consistent output from a model
options.B: The process of permanently updating a model's internal weights through additional training
options.C: The technique of compressing a model's parameters to reduce memory footprint
options.D: The process of converting text into a numerical vector for similarity search

questions.explanation: Prompt engineering is the deliberate practice of designing prompts to reliably improve the accuracy, consistency, or usefulness of a model's output, and the chapter calls it the highest-leverage, lowest-cost lever for reducing spend. Option B describes fine-tuning, a fundamentally different and more expensive approach. Option C describes model quantization. Option D describes creating an embedding, unrelated to how a prompt itself is written.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: How does few-shot prompting differ from zero-shot prompting in terms of cost?

options.A: Few-shot prompting reduces the number of tokens needed because the model requires less explanation
options.B: Few-shot prompting only affects the length of the model's generated output, not its input
options.C: Few-shot and zero-shot prompting always cost exactly the same because the task is identical
options.D: Few-shot prompting includes worked examples in the prompt, consuming additional input tokens on every request compared to zero-shot's plain instruction

questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting prepends a small number of worked examples before the actual task, and each example consumes real input tokens on every single request, unlike zero-shot's bare instruction. Option A reverses the cost effect; few-shot costs more, not less. Option B is incorrect because few-shot's added cost falls on input tokens, not output length. Option C ignores the token cost difference the chapter explicitly quantifies.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: Why does chain-of-thought prompting typically increase cost in a different way than few-shot prompting does?

options.A: It increases the number of examples included in the prompt, not the length of the response
options.B: It increases the length of the model's generated output, since the reasoning steps themselves are generated text, rather than adding input tokens
options.C: It requires a vector database to store reasoning steps
options.D: It has no effect on token cost because reasoning happens internally without generating text

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason through intermediate steps before its final answer, and those reasoning steps are generated text that lengthens the output, unlike few-shot's added input tokens. Option A describes few-shot prompting, not chain-of-thought. Option C invents a dependency on retrieval infrastructure that the technique does not require. Option D is false; the reasoning steps are visible, billed output tokens.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: What is model hallucination?

options.A: A deliberate error introduced by a provider to test system robustness
options.B: The delay between sending a request and receiving a response
options.C: The process of retrieving relevant text from an external source before answering
options.D: A confident, fluent, plausible-sounding response that is factually wrong or entirely fabricated

questions.explanation: Model hallucination is a confident, fluent, plausible-sounding response that is factually wrong or entirely fabricated, arising because models predict statistically likely next words rather than consulting a source of truth. Option A wrongly frames it as intentional testing rather than a structural risk. Option B describes model latency. Option C describes retrieval, the technique used to reduce hallucination, not hallucination itself.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?

options.A: To reduce hallucination by grounding the model's response in text retrieved from an external source before generating an answer
options.B: To permanently update a model's weights with new information
options.C: To reduce a model's memory footprint by lowering numerical precision
options.D: To increase a model's context window size automatically

questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant text from an external source and inserts it into the prompt before the model answers, grounding the response in verifiable material and sharply reducing, though not eliminating, hallucination on covered topics. Option B describes fine-tuning, not RAG, which changes nothing about the model's weights. Option C describes model quantization. Option D confuses RAG with a context-window change, which RAG does not perform.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: What role does a vector database play in a RAG pipeline?

options.A: It permanently stores the model's trained parameters
options.B: It stores millions of embeddings and quickly returns the stored text most similar in meaning to a new query
options.C: It converts a user's query into a fluent natural-language response
options.D: It tracks distinct, identifiable releases of a model over time

questions.explanation: A vector database is built to hold millions of embeddings and answer, in milliseconds, which stored pieces of text are most similar in meaning to a new query, making fast retrieval possible. Option A describes where a model's own weights live, not a vector database. Option C describes what the language model itself does, not the database. Option D describes model versioning, an unrelated deployment practice.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: A deployment team turns on batch inference and observes that system-wide throughput doubles while individual request latency increases significantly. What is the underlying reason for this trade-off?

options.A: Batch inference reduces the total number of tokens generated per request
options.B: Batch inference switches the model to a smaller, distilled version automatically
options.C: Batch inference processes multiple requests together in a single pass, improving total work done per unit of GPU time, but an individual request may wait for a batch to fill before processing begins
options.D: Batch inference eliminates the need for a vector database in retrieval tasks

questions.explanation: Batch inference groups multiple requests into a single pass through the model, which raises throughput by getting more total work done per unit of GPU time, but an individual request may sit waiting for its batch to fill, raising that request's latency. Option A misattributes the effect to token count rather than processing structure. Option B confuses batching with knowledge distillation. Option D is unrelated; batching has no bearing on retrieval infrastructure.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: A financial services company has strict data-privacy requirements, substantial upfront capital available, and an experienced in-house infrastructure team. Which deployment approach best matches these circumstances?

options.A: Cloud-hosted deployment, trading upfront capital for ongoing operating expense and less control
options.B: On-premises deployment, maximizing control over data privacy by running the model on infrastructure the company owns and operates
options.C: Knowledge distillation, to train a smaller student model from a larger teacher model
options.D: Zero-shot prompting, to avoid the cost of writing worked examples

questions.explanation: On-premises deployment maximizes control over data privacy and lets an organization fully own hardware costs, at the price of significant upfront capital and in-house expertise — exactly the profile this company has. Option A describes the opposite trade-off, favored by teams without capital or infrastructure staff. Option C addresses model size and cost, not deployment location. Option D is a prompting technique, unrelated to where a model physically runs.

questions.chapter: Prompting, Deployment, and Model Optimization Basics
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes model right-sizing?

options.A: Reducing the numerical precision used to store a model's parameters
options.B: Training a new, smaller model to mimic the outputs of a larger teacher model
options.C: Increasing a model's context window to handle longer documents
options.D: Deliberately choosing the smallest, cheapest model that still meets accuracy and latency requirements for a given task, rather than defaulting to the largest available model

questions.explanation: Model right-sizing is the discipline of deliberately choosing the smallest, cheapest model that still meets a task's accuracy and latency requirements, rather than defaulting to the largest, most capable, and most expensive option. Option A describes model quantization. Option B describes knowledge distillation, a related but distinct technique. Option C is unrelated to matching model choice to task difficulty.
